questions.q: Define coefficient of restitution (e) for a 1D collision. State its values for perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic, and partially inelastic collisions.
questions.a: Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂f - v₁f)/(v₁i - v₂i) = relative speed of separation / relative speed of approach. For perfectly elastic: e = 1; perfectly inelastic (bodies stick): e = 0; partially inelastic: 0 < e < 1. A wrong answer (e.g., e = v₁f/v₁i or confusing e with energy ratio) reveals the student doesn't understand e is defined via relative velocities, not absolute velocities or energy fractions.

questions.q: A ball of mass m moving at speed v collides head-on with an identical ball at rest. After collision, the first ball stops and the second moves at speed v. Is this collision elastic or inelastic? Justify using both momentum and kinetic energy.
questions.a: Elastic. Momentum: initial = mv, final = mv (conserved). Kinetic energy: initial = ½mv², final = ½mv² (conserved). Since both conserved, e = 1. A student saying "inelastic because the first ball stopped" confuses velocity transfer with energy loss — they must check energy conservation explicitly, not assume stopping implies energy loss.

questions.q: A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s collides head-on with a stationary 3 kg block. After collision, the 2 kg block moves at -1 m/s (rebounds). Find the velocity of the 3 kg block and the coefficient of restitution.
questions.a: Momentum conservation: (2)(4) + (3)(0) = (2)(-1) + (3)v₂f → 8 = -2 + 3v₂f → v₂f = 10/3 ≈ 3.33 m/s. Coefficient of restitution: e = (v₂f - v₁f)/(v₁i - v₂i) = (10/3 - (-1))/(4 - 0) = (13/3)/4 = 13/12 ≈ 1.08. Since e > 1, this collision is physically impossible (violates energy conservation). A student getting e > 1 but not recognizing impossibility fails to connect e ≤ 1 with energy conservation — they must check if K_f ≤ Kᵢ.

questions.q: Two identical balls undergo a 1D elastic collision. Ball A has initial velocity +5 m/s, Ball B has initial velocity -3 m/s. Without calculation, state the final velocities. Explain the physical principle.
questions.a: For equal masses in 1D elastic collision, velocities exchange: v_Af = -3 m/s, v_Bf = +5 m/s. Principle: In center-of-mass frame, equal masses simply reverse velocities in elastic collision; transforming back to lab frame gives exchange. A student attempting to use formulas v₁f = [(m₁-m₂)/(m₁+m₂)]v₁i + ... without recognizing the symmetry wastes time and misses the conceptual shortcut — they haven't internalized the physical meaning of elastic collision for equal masses.

questions.q: A student claims: "In any inelastic collision, kinetic energy is lost, so momentum cannot be conserved." Evaluate this statement and correct the misconception.
questions.a: Statement is FALSE. Momentum is ALWAYS conserved in an isolated system (no external forces) because internal forces are equal and opposite (Newton's 3rd law) regardless of collision type. Kinetic energy is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions because internal forces do non-conservative work (deformation → heat/sound). The student confuses "energy not conserved" with "momentum not conserved" — they must distinguish between vector quantity (momentum, conserved if ΣF_ext = 0) and scalar energy (conserved only if internal forces are conservative).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a ramp, two marbles of different masses, and a measuring tape to determine the coefficient of restitution for marble-marble collisions. Describe procedure, measurements, and calculation.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Place target marble at rest on horizontal track. (2) Roll incident marble from known height h on ramp; measure its speed v₁i at bottom using v = √(2gh) or photogate. (3) After collision, measure distances traveled by both marbles in time t (using video or stopwatch) to get v₁f, v₂f. (4) Compute e = (v₂f - v₁f)/(v₁i - 0). Repeat for different masses. A poor answer measures only final speeds without initial speed, or assumes e = height ratio (which works only for ball-floor collisions, not ball-ball) — revealing confusion between different collision geometries.
